cards.title: E. Gerald Corrigan
cards.sub: 1985 · Federal Reserve Bank of New York
cards.body: President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Not a monetary-policy week: he held Fedwire open past midnight, signed off a special loan agreement negotiated mid-crisis, and later testified to a House subcommittee that the Fed had been "prudent, disciplined and appropriate" — and "a bit lucky".
cards.prompt: Late 1985: a clearing bank's records are corrupt but its counterparties keep delivering, and the Fed has already lent it more than the bank is worth. Name the New York Fed president in the chair, and the blunt lever he reached for the next morning when lending had stopped working.
cards.answer: E. Gerald Corrigan. At about 11:30 a.m. on Friday 22 November 1985 the New York Fed temporarily stopped accepting securities transfers for the Bank of New York's account — roughly 90 minutes of shutting off the inbound flow, because nothing else stopped the overdraft growing.

cards.title: The Bank of New York ledger overflow
cards.body: Volume past 32,000 government securities issues broke recently installed software and damaged BoNY's database of accounts and transactions. Chairman J. Carter Bacot described the fix as the electronic equivalent of patching a tire; it failed after midnight. Interest cost about $5 million, near 7 percent of nine months' earnings. Total assets: $15.9 billion.
cards.prompt: One clearing bank, one Thursday, and a delivery-versus-payment wire that never pauses. Name the bank, the wire and the dates — then the two dollar figures: the peak overdraft, and the overnight central-bank credit that closed it.
cards.answer: The Bank of New York, on Fedwire, 20–22 November 1985. The overdraft reached $32 billion by the Thursday evening as the testimony was reported at the time; the Richmond Fed's 2015 reconstruction of the same hearing puts it at nearly $30 billion at 8:30 p.m. The New York Fed's discount-window advance was $22.6 billion, and a further $1 billion overnight overdraft appeared when BoNY misjudged its own position — $23.6 billion of total credit, secured by every asset of the bank plus customer securities, book value about $36 billion.

cards.title: Economic Brief EB15-05
cards.body: Five pages, endnoted to the December 12, 1985 House Banking subcommittee hearing and to contemporaneous Wall Street Journal and American Banker reporting. Source of the clock: the software problem known at 11:30 a.m., over $20 billion of overdraft by 2:15 p.m., nearly $30 billion by 8:30 p.m., the wires held open to 2:15 a.m.
cards.prompt: You want the BoNY failure hour by hour with the Fed's own numbers rather than a retelling. Which short 2015 Richmond Fed publication carries it, and what does it argue the episode is a clean case study of?
cards.answer: Huberto M. Ennis and David A. Price, "Discount Window Lending: Policy Trade-offs and the 1985 BoNY Computer Failure", Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Economic Brief EB15-05, May 2015. It reads the episode as a case study in when discount-window intervention is justified on efficiency grounds, and in the moral hazard that follows — rescue expected, operational safety under-bought.

cards.title: Pricing the gap between effect and record
cards.body: A bank that could not produce its own ledger financed the gap below market. The argument that followed is the one every payments team inherits: if the record can fail while the money keeps moving, the cost of the gap has to land on whoever chose not to close it.
cards.prompt: BoNY borrowed roughly 1.5 times its total assets overnight from the discount window. Was that emergency money expensive or cheap relative to the market — and what did the two Fed officials who testified want changed because of it?
cards.answer: Cheap. The 7.5 percent discount rate BoNY paid was less than the prevailing federal funds rate; only the extra $1 billion overdraft drew a penalty rate. Volcker and Corrigan both supported charging a penalty rate for lending caused by an operational failure, and the Fed generalised penalty pricing for discount-window lending in a 2003 policy change.
